summary: The Ordinances and Rules Committee voted 5-0 to recommend a battery storage zoning amendment, as amended, for the Oct 13, 2026 council meeting.

Brookfield prohibited all battery storage in every district through Nov 30, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it for lacking justification, for unlawful scope, for conflicting with the consolidated permit law, and for procedural defects.

article: Proposed Chapter 181 amendment: temporary moratorium on commercial battery storage
summary: The Planning Board asked the City Council to adopt a temporary zoning moratorium on locally regulated commercial battery storage. It was on the council's Oct 6, 2026 agenda.

Gill's Article 7 imposed a moratorium on battery storage and data centers until May 3, 2027. The Attorney General disapproved the battery storage part but approved the data-center part, since data centers are not a protected use.

article: Article 7 (May 4, 2026 Annual Town Meeting), data-center part
summary: The same letter approved the data-center half of Gill's Article 7: a moratorium on data centers until May 3, 2027 stands, because data centers aren't a protected use. The battery-storage half was struck.
Chesterfield adopted a battery storage moratorium through Sep 30, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it for lacking any health, safety or welfare justification.

Templeton's Article 38, a citizen petition, put a 360-day moratorium on constructing new data centers, through May 8, 2027, while the town studies their effect on police, fire and other emergency services, schools, water, sewer and roads. The Attorney General approved it: a temporary moratorium with a legitimate zoning purpose doesn't conflict with state law.

Barre's battery storage bylaw was approved except a requirement to eliminate any view of the facility, pesticide bans, conditioning site plan approval on other boards' approvals, and a $100 million insurance requirement.
Upton allowed small-scale ground-mounted solar as an accessory use in residential districts with site plan approval. The Attorney General approved it.
Hanson made further battery storage amendments. The Attorney General approved them.

Lee adopted a moratorium on commercial battery storage through Nov 14, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it for lacking justification and conflicting with the consolidated permit requirement starting Oct 1, 2026.
Millis defined battery storage and data storage centers and set the districts where battery storage is allowed or prohibited. The Attorney General approved it.

technology: small clean energy projects, including battery storage
summary: Southborough's new Industrial Park district allows small clean energy infrastructure uses, including battery storage, subject to state siting rules. The Attorney General approved it, with comments on the consolidated permit law.
Ashby adopted a tiered battery storage section. The Attorney General approved it.

Medway adopted a Consolidated Local Permit section for small clean energy facilities to conform to the 2024 Climate Act and 225 CMR 29.00. The Attorney General approved it; it is the only decision tagged Small Clean Energy Facilities in the portal as of Oct 10, 2026.

Petersham's revised solar and battery storage zoning was approved except a rule that battery storage not be visible from public roads and a requirement that owners pay for emergency-responder equipment and training.

Sturbridge adopted a moratorium on standalone battery storage of 250 kWh or more through Dec 1, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it for lacking justification, being unlimited in scope, and conflicting with the requirement to accept consolidated permit applications from Oct 1, 2026.

article: Sunpin Energy Services, LLC v. Zoning Board of Appeals of Petersham, 497 Mass. 794 (Supreme Judicial Court-13860)
outcome: ruled for the developer; sent back to the board
summary: The Supreme Judicial Court held that a town must give solar reasonable opportunities and may deny a special permit for a protected solar project only when necessary to protect public health, safety or welfare. It vacated the Land Court judgment that had upheld Petersham’s denial and sent the matter back to the zoning board to decide under that test. The Appeals Court (105 Mass. App. Ct. 641, July 9, 2025) had ordered the permit issued.
Becket adopted a moratorium on large solar and battery storage through Sep 30, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it for lacking a health, safety or welfare justification.

Worthington adopted a town-wide moratorium on large ground-mounted solar and battery storage over 600 kWh through June 30, 2027. The Attorney General disapproved it for lacking a health, safety or welfare justification.

Worthington's limited-area moratoriums on large solar (Art. 7) and on large energy storage (Art. 8) were disapproved because they were not limited in scope or time; the Attorney General also struck Art. 8's ban on storage over 5 MWh as unreasonable.

Whately barred battery storage over 250 kWh of aggregate capacity in its Aquifer Protection District and added battery storage definitions. The Attorney General approved it without comment; the letter does not describe the article, so its content comes from news coverage.
Egremont's development-standards amendments were approved except solar site design text requiring that power from a solar facility be used solely by the property owners.
Monson's large-solar amendments (Art. 30) were approved except minimum lot sizes tied to array size, and its new battery storage provisions (Art. 31) were approved.

Southwick adopted a moratorium on large solar and battery storage through May 31, 2027. The Attorney General disapproved it for lacking any health, safety or welfare justification and for procedural defects.
Colrain amended its large-scale ground-mounted solar rules. The Attorney General approved them.

article: Town of Wendell v. Campbell, No. 25 MISC 000014 (LER) (Mass. Land Ct. Mar 12, 2026)
summary: The Land Court upheld the Attorney General’s Nov 14, 2024 disapproval of Wendell’s general (licensing) bylaw for battery storage: its effect on land use was predominant, so it had to be adopted as a zoning bylaw under G.L. c. 40A, § 5, and a licensing bylaw could not be used to get around the solar protections in § 3. Decided March 12, 2026.

Blandford adopted a moratorium on large ground-mounted solar and battery storage through May 31, 2026. The Attorney General disapproved it, noting that it had approved a Blandford solar moratorium in 2019 but has disapproved such moratoriums since Tracer Lane II.

article: Zoning Ordinance Section 5-31, Interim Restriction for battery storage
summary: Westfield made battery storage a prohibited use in all districts as an interim restriction, adopted Feb 26, 2026 and running through Sep 30, 2026; it has now expired. As a city ordinance it never went to the Attorney General, and the moratoriums the Attorney General strikes for towns have no counterpart review for cities.
Medway required commercial battery storage operators to submit third-party safety certification before operating. The Attorney General approved it, with comments on the 2024 Climate Act.
After its 2024 moratorium was struck, Hampden adopted a battery storage section. The Attorney General approved it.

Leyden allowed commercial or industrial-scale battery facilities by special permit. The Attorney General approved it but flagged unclear wording and its earlier disapproval of Leyden's standalone-battery storage ban.

Shutesbury's Article 10 put a temporary moratorium on building new data centers until June 20, 2026, added a definition of "data center" and listed data centers as a prohibited use in every zoning district. The Attorney General approved it: data centers aren't a protected use, so a time-limited moratorium with a planning purpose stands.
Boxford added a Battery Energy Storage Systems section. The Attorney General approved it.

article: Article 1 (June 16, 2025 Annual Town Meeting; zoning recodification)
summary: Paxton's recodified zoning was partially approved; Section 11, allowing large ground-mounted solar with site plan approval, was approved with a warning not to apply it to deny solar or battery storage.
Hubbardston's second battery storage bylaw, adopted after its near-total ban was struck in 2023, was approved.

Uxbridge's large-scale solar and battery storage amendments were approved except a unilateral extension of the 35-day review period and a rule allowing denial if project revenue would not cover town costs.

article: Article 36 (May 19, 2025 Annual Town Meeting; zoning recodification)
summary: Holden's recodified zoning, including Section 7.4 allowing solar array fields as of right with site plan review in three districts, was approved as to its solar provisions.
Rutland added a battery storage Facilities article. The Attorney General approved it.
Shelburne's battery storage amendments were approved except a herbicide ban.
Wareham allowed large solar and battery storage in its Business Development Overlay District. The Attorney General approved it over an opposition letter, with comments on the 2024 Climate Act.

article: Article 45 (May 6, 2025 Annual Town Meeting; zoning recodification)
summary: Billerica's recodified zoning, including Section 6.5 on solar energy conversion systems, was approved (an unrelated sign provision was disapproved).
Tewksbury defined battery storage and allowed it by special permit in its two industrial districts and Office-Research district. The Attorney General approved it.
Hardwick amended its use table and solar facility section and its battery storage rules. The Attorney General approved them despite procedural objections from a Select Board member.
Merrimac added battery storage definitions and regulations. The Attorney General approved them.
Groveland amended its battery storage section. The Attorney General approved the changes.
West Newbury adopted a battery storage section with procedures and performance standards. The Attorney General approved it.
Southampton's solar amendments were approved except a ban on herbicides, pesticides and chemical fertilizers at solar facilities.
Rochester's new battery storage chapter was approved except its noise limits, which the Attorney General found to be an unreasonable regulation.
Rochester's follow-up amendments to its battery storage chapter, including special permit rules in water-related districts, were approved.

After the Attorney General struck its 2024 ban on earth removal for energy storage, Hadley limited earth removal to what is incidental and necessary to build a solar system. The Attorney General approved this narrower rule.

article: Duxbury Energy Storage, LLC v. Town of Duxbury Zoning Board of Appeals, Land Ct. 23 MISC 000643 (LER)
summary: The Land Court held that a standalone battery facility not connected to any solar is a structure that facilitates the collection of solar energy, so it is protected by § 3, and annulled the town's denial. The Attorney General has cited it in battery storage decisions since September 2025 (Rochester, Case #11532).
Alford's 2019 Solar Energy Systems section for small, medium and large ground-mounted systems was approved in 2025.
Hampden adopted a six-month moratorium on permits for stand-alone battery storage. The Attorney General disapproved it as unsupported by any health, safety or welfare justification.
Ludlow allowed Tier 1 battery storage by right everywhere and larger tiers by special permit in specified districts. The Attorney General approved it.

Acushnet's new general Stormwater Management bylaw specifically requires large-scale ground-mounted solar to obtain a stormwater permit. The Attorney General approved it, cautioning the town to apply the solar provisions consistently with § 3. Unlike Wendell's and Shutesbury's licensing bylaws, it regulates a stormwater impact rather than land use.
After its 2023 moratorium was struck, Hanson allowed Tier I battery storage by right everywhere and Tier II by right with site plan review in three of six districts. The Attorney General approved it.
Lunenburg regulated battery storage both as part of solar facilities and as a standalone use. The Attorney General approved it.
Needham amended several zoning sections on solar energy systems, including medium-scale ground-mounted solar. The Attorney General approved them.

Shutesbury's general bylaw required a license from a new seven-member Energy Storage System Licensing Board to operate any non-residential storage system. It was disapproved because it regulated land use and should have been adopted as zoning.
Belchertown added a battery storage section with siting, design, monitoring and removal standards. The Attorney General approved it.
Wendell's citizen-petitioned general bylaw to license battery storage was disapproved because it regulated land use and should have been adopted as zoning. The Land Court upheld this in March 2026.
Hadley's energy storage definitions and Large Energy Storage Systems section were approved except a ban on earth removal to facilitate an ESS installation.

Northfield adopted moratoriums on principal-use battery storage and on large ground-mounted solar, including agrivoltaics, through August 2025. The Attorney General disapproved both moratoriums (it approved a new battery storage definition in Art. 26).
Sunderland amended its zoning to allow and regulate battery energy storage facilities. The Attorney General approved it.
Groveland required site plan review for battery storage and added a battery storage section. The Attorney General approved both.

Northborough's new Highway Business Southwest district prohibits large-scale ground-mounted solar. The Attorney General approved it as a single-district rule but told the town to apply it consistently with § 3.
Hinsdale adopted an Electric Energy Storage Systems section allowing storage by special permit in all districts. The Attorney General approved it.
Wilbraham amended several zoning sections to regulate battery storage. The Attorney General approved them as consistent with § 3.
Princeton added a Solar Energy Systems section for small and large systems. The Attorney General approved it.
Dover allowed small and medium ground-mounted solar by right with site plan review in all districts except its Conservancy district. The Attorney General approved it.
Spencer's replacement solar and battery storage regulations were approved except rules on herbicides, pesticides and fertilizers at agrivoltaic installations.

Spencer's temporary moratoriums on large ground-mounted solar and on energy systems as a principal use were never ruled on. The Attorney General took no action because the town adopted solar and storage zoning in May 2024, which ended the moratoriums by their own terms.
Blandford adopted a new battery storage section and added Tier 1-3 battery storage to its Schedule of Uses. The Attorney General approved both; a related Article 5 was put on procedural hold.
Blandford's new Schedule of Uses sorts ground-mounted solar into small, medium and large categories with permit paths. The Attorney General approved it, with § 3 comments.
Lenox replaced its large-scale solar section with a Ground-Mounted Solar Installations section and exempted rooftop panels from height limits. The Attorney General approved it.
Lunenburg allowed solar parking canopies by special permit in its Commercial and Office Park/Industrial districts. The Attorney General approved it.

Wareham's battery storage rules were approved except provisions limiting battery storage to systems tied to large-scale solar, which amounted to a complete ban on principal-use (standalone) battery storage.
Leyden's large-scale solar section was approved except prohibitions on battery energy storage facilities (effectively a standalone-battery storage ban) and a herbicide ban.

article: Article 7 (Nov 6, 2023 Special Town Meeting; zoning recodification)
summary: Westhampton's new zoning bylaw was largely approved, but the Attorney General disapproved Section 5.14(2), which capped medium and large solar arrays at 1.5 acres, as an unreasonable regulation.
Sherborn's new large-scale solar overlay district and bylaw were approved except text prohibiting non-accessory battery storage.
Dracut amended its solar PV facility and battery storage rules. The Attorney General approved both.

Hanson's battery storage article imposed a two-year town-wide moratorium on Tier 1 battery storage and allowed Tier 2 only in an overlay district that was never mapped. The Attorney General disapproved the whole article.

article: Article 33 (May 9, 2023 Annual Town Meeting; zoning recodification)
summary: Southampton's zoning recodification was approved except, among other items, a ban on herbicides, pesticides and commercial fertilizers at solar installations.
Becket's 2019 amendments to its solar PV section were approved in 2024. The Attorney General noted that a pesticide provision already in the bylaw would be preempted.
Norwell's new solar bylaw was approved except several provisions, including a visual-impact requirement, which the Attorney General found unreasonable under § 3 or preempted.
Lanesborough allowed accessory solar and storage by right everywhere, and utility-scale solar and non-accessory storage by special permit in all districts. The Attorney General approved it.
West Newbury replaced its large-scale solar overlay district with location criteria. The Attorney General approved it.

article: Article 5 (June 28, 2023 Special Town Meeting; zoning recodification)
summary: Erving's recodified zoning allows accessory energy storage everywhere, other ESS by special permit in two districts, and regulates solar. The Attorney General approved these sections; it disapproved unrelated text.
Shrewsbury's large-scale solar and battery storage section was approved except a requirement that battery facilities be owned or operated by the town or its municipal light plant.

Hubbardston's Grid-Scale battery storage article imposed what the Attorney General called an almost complete ban on grid-scale battery storage, with no record evidence of need. The Attorney General disapproved it in its entirety.
The Attorney General approved Hubbardston's use-table clean-ups except references to the disapproved grid-scale battery storage article and a pesticide/herbicide ban at solar sites.
After its 2022 moratorium was struck, Ware adopted a battery storage zoning section with definitions, an aquifer-district rule and use-table entries. The Attorney General approved it.
Sharon replaced Section 7.7, Solar Photovoltaic Installations, allowing roof, canopy and ground-mounted solar of all sizes broadly by right or with site plan review. The Attorney General approved it.
Charlemont amended its Use Table for solar uses, including height limits and permit paths. The Attorney General approved it, with comments on § 3.

Pelham's rewritten solar bylaw was approved except carbon-sequestration mitigation, a cap on installations in the overlay district, a pesticide ban, a rule barring solar-sited storage from handling off-site energy, and a requirement that storage owners pay for emergency-responder training.
The Attorney General approved Pelham's new energy storage system definition (Art. 29) but disapproved Art. 30, which prohibited ESS as a principal use in every district.

Shutesbury's new solar bylaw, which also banned energy storage as a principal use in all districts, was disapproved in full. The Planning Board notice was defective, and limiting large solar to one per planning sector violated § 3 and the uniformity rule.
Carver's large-scale solar amendments were approved except a cap of five acres of deforestation per lot and herbicide/pesticide rules.
Carver added Tier 1-3 battery storage requirements and listed where each tier is allowed by right, by special permit or prohibited. The Attorney General approved it.
Hanson allowed small and medium ground-mounted solar as of right with site plan review. The Attorney General approved it.

Acushnet replaced its large-scale ground-mounted solar article, and the Attorney General approved it. The letter notes that a 180-day solar moratorium voted in spring 2022 was never submitted for Attorney General review and so never took lawful effect.
Lancaster allowed standalone energy storage systems by special permit in all districts. The Attorney General approved it.
Salisbury adopted a new ground-mounted solar zoning bylaw. The Attorney General approved it, to be applied consistently with § 3.
Whately required solar utility connections to be underground where feasible. The Attorney General approved it.
Mashpee's solar rules, including medium and large solar by special permit in its C-1 and C-2 districts, were approved except a ban on herbicides, pesticides and chemical fertilizers.

Wareham's rewritten solar bylaw was approved except several provisions, including a visual-impact requirement, an alternative-site analysis, a limit on battery storage, consultant-selection rules and a herbicide ban.
Harwich allowed accessory residential rooftop and ground-mounted solar by right, subject to setback, height and screening standards. The Attorney General approved it.

Tyngsborough's new Table of Uses allows small, medium and large ground-mounted solar as of right with site plan review in residential districts (large-scale elsewhere by Planning Board special permit). The Attorney General approved it.
Warren amended the documents required for solar site plans in its Solar Energy section. The Attorney General approved the change.
Medway amended its ground-mounted solar definition and vegetation-control rules. The Attorney General approved them, with comments.
Douglas's new Solar By-law for commercial and residential systems was approved except a herbicide ban, which is preempted.
Spencer's solar amendments were approved except a ban on energy storage systems as a principal use in every district and a cap of 25 large-scale solar facilities town-wide.
Medway's battery storage and solar amendments were approved except Schedule of Uses text that banned Tier 2 battery storage in every district but one.

article: NextSun Energy LLC v. Fernandes, No. 19 MISC 000230 (RBF) (Mass. Land Ct. May 9, 2023)
summary: The Land Court held that a battery energy storage system built with a solar project in Norton is a structure that facilitates the collection of solar energy, so it has the § 3 solar protections (decision May 9, 2023; amended judgment entered June 23, 2023). The Attorney General has cited it in solar and battery-storage decisions since September 2023.
Rochester added year-round screening and buffer requirements for large-scale solar. The Attorney General approved them but warned they cannot be used to deny otherwise compliant projects.
New Marlborough amended its solar section, including new rules for small-scale ground-mounted systems. The Attorney General approved it, to be applied consistently with § 3.

Ware adopted a roughly 13-month moratorium on battery storage even though it had regulated battery storage since 2020. The Attorney General disapproved it as unsupported by health or safety evidence and not adopted for a legitimate planning purpose.
Ashfield replaced its large-scale solar section with a tiered Ground-Mounted Photovoltaic Facilities bylaw. The Attorney General approved it, to be applied consistently with § 3.
Sandwich allowed large solar canopies over parking and walkways as of right in all districts. The Attorney General approved it because it promotes solar.

Wendell's ground-mounted solar and energy-facility bylaw was approved except its herbicide rules and its complete ban on stand-alone battery storage in all districts. The Attorney General said the ban was not backed by health, safety or welfare evidence.
Dighton's new Solar Electric Generating Facilities section was approved except a herbicide ban, which is preempted.

Manchester-by-the-Sea recodified its use regulations into a new Table of Uses, including solar uses. The Attorney General approved it and told the town to apply its existing solar provisions consistently with § 3.

Falmouth's recodified zoning was approved except, for large-scale solar in its overlay district, a ban on siting on land deforested within the prior five years, which the Attorney General called little different from an absolute prohibition.

Oakham capped battery storage at half the capacity of an associated large solar installation and prohibited battery storage not attached to a permitted large-scale solar site. The Attorney General approved it; within weeks (Wendell, Mar 2023) the office began disapproving similar standalone-battery storage bans.

Arlington required certain projects to include rooftop solar covering the equivalent of at least half the roof area. The Attorney General approved it because it promotes solar and does not conflict with the Building Code.
Athol's changes to its Tier 2 and Tier 3 battery storage rules were approved except text exempting smaller systems from building, electrical and fire permits, which state codes preempt.

Boxborough's medium and large ground-mounted solar bylaw was approved except a ban on siting solar on land deforested within the prior five years, which the Attorney General called an unreasonable regulation.

Oxford added a Large Scale Battery Energy Storage Systems chapter allowing battery storage by special permit with site plan approval in its Light Industrial and Industrial districts. The Attorney General approved it.
Belchertown's new commercial solar bylaw was approved except a ban on herbicides, rodenticides and other pesticides, which is preempted.

Carver adopted a one-year ban on new or expanded large-scale solar (Art. 26) and an 11.5-month ban on battery storage (Art. 38). The Attorney General disapproved both because they were not grounded in articulated health, safety or welfare concerns.
Middleborough added its Commercial Development district to the Solar Overlay District and allowed accessory and large-scale solar there under conditions. The Attorney General approved it.

article: Article 29 (May 2, 2022 Annual Town Meeting; zoning recodification)
summary: Tewksbury's recodified zoning includes a large-scale solar section that cuts the minimum lot from 20 to 5 acres and allows such solar by special permit in all districts. The Attorney General approved it, noting the Table of Uses had not been updated to match; unrelated text was disapproved.

Montague defined battery storage, allowed battery facilities by special permit in its industrial districts, allowed small systems as an accessory use everywhere, and encouraged co-location with solar. The Attorney General approved it.

article: Tracer Lane II Realty, LLC v. City of Waltham, 489 Mass. 775 (Supreme Judicial Court-13195)
summary: The Supreme Judicial Court held that Waltham's ban on large-scale solar in all but 1-2% of the city was impermissible, and that § 3 claims require balancing the town's interest against the burden on solar. Every Attorney General solar or battery storage decision since mid-2022 relies on it.

Medway's time-limited moratorium on battery storage construction in its Energy Resource district was approved because it was limited in time and geographic scope and served a planning purpose. This is the only clean-energy moratorium the Attorney General approved in 2022-2026, and it came two weeks before the Supreme Judicial Court's Tracer Lane II ruling.
Hopkinton's new commercial solar bylaw (special permit, lots of 3+ acres) was approved except a ban on pesticides, herbicides and synthetic fertilizers, which state law preempts.
Washington designated a parcel where large-scale solar is allowed as of right, keeping special permits elsewhere. The Attorney General approved it because it promotes rather than limits solar.

Wareham limited large ground-mounted solar to parcels of 10 acres or less that had been cleared for at least five years. The Attorney General disapproved it as an unreasonable solar regulation with no health, safety or welfare record, and as an improper open-ended moratorium.
Amendments to Spencer's solar PV bylaw on decommissioning surety, setbacks and visual mitigation were approved. The Attorney General cautioned the town to apply them consistently with § 3.

West Brookfield added dimensional and design standards for battery storage accessory to solar facilities. The Attorney General approved it, with comments on how the decommissioning fee must be handled.
Deerfield replaced its Section 3800 solar energy systems bylaw. The Attorney General approved it but warned the town to apply it consistently with the solar protections in G.L. c. 40A, § 3.

article: Article 4 (Oct 1, 2026 Special Town Meeting), Clean Energy zoning section
summary: Lee voters unanimously approved a Clean Energy zoning section with revised solar and wind rules and the town's first battery storage rules, based on the state energy department’s model, after the Attorney General struck Lee's battery storage moratorium. No Attorney General decision as of Oct 10, 2026.
